content.text: Thomas Paine’s later life saw him move from revolutionary prominence to poverty, religious controversy, and social ostracism. After living with the Bonnevilles in Paris, he travelled to Belgium, returned to Paris, and sailed from Havre to Baltimore in 1802, then visited Washington, Bordentown, New York, Stonington, and his farm at New Rochelle. He defended republicanism, deism, abolition, Louisiana’s purchase, and neutral commerce, while pursuing bridge and steam inventions. In America he faced mobs, denied voting rights, financial hardship, illness, and slander from Cheetham and Carver. He died peacefully in Greenwich, New York, in 1809, maintaining his beliefs; his remains were later exhumed by Cobbett. The appended fiction follows Frank Blaisdell, whose lost fortune restores him to useful work, while the Blaisdell family relocates to Plainville. Miss Maggie and Mr. Smith finally confess love, though Smith’s identity as Stanley Fulton remains startlingly undisclosed.
